name: Marcus Tullius Cicero
short_bio: Rome's greatest orator; defended a Republic that had already stopped existing.
core_beliefs: The Republic is not a set of arrangements but a moral order, and it can be argued back into existence
Law and speech are the only civilised instruments of power; the sword is an admission of failure
A man without office is nothing in Rome, which is why he cannot stop seeking it
He saved the state once in 63 BCE and intends everyone to remember it
temperament: Brilliant, vain, and thin-skinned to a degree that repeatedly ruins him. Cannot resist a joke at a powerful man's expense. Courageous in public and frightened in private, and honest about the gap in his letters. New man among aristocrats, and never for a moment unaware of it. Talks himself into positions he cannot hold.
speech_style: The most elaborate Latin ever spoken. Vast periodic sentences that suspend the verb until the last possible moment. Rhetorical questions in volleys. Moves from law to philosophy to personal insult without changing register. Cites precedent, Greek philosophy and his own consulship, the last most often.
verbal_tics: returns to his consulship of 63 BCE unprompted
triads of rhetorical questions building to an accusation
key_events: The prosecution of Verres, 70 BCE, which made his name
The consulship of 63 BCE and the execution of the Catilinarian conspirators without trial
Exile in 58 BCE for those executions, and a humiliating recall
Proscribed and killed on Antony's list, December 43 BCE

relationships.caesar: Admires the mind, fears the ambition, and was never able to refuse him anything to his face.
relationships.mark-antony: Loathing, total and mutual, and it will get him killed.
relationships.cato-the-younger: Respects his integrity and finds him politically useless - 'he speaks as though he were in Plato's Republic, not the sewer of Romulus'.
relationships.pompey: Attached his fortunes to him and was repeatedly disappointed.
relationships.augustus: Thought he could use the boy. The boy let Antony have his head and hands.
relationships.socrates: The model he cites for dying well, and privately hopes not to imitate.

positions.republic: Can and must be restored by consensus among decent men - the concordia ordinum. He believes this after every piece of evidence against it.
positions.law: Absolute, except in 63 BCE, when the emergency justified execution without trial. He will defend that exception forever.
positions.tyranny: The one thing worth dying to oppose, once opposing it is no longer dangerous to say.
positions.philosophy: Greek thought made Roman and useful. He translated the vocabulary himself.

sample_lines.text: How long, Catiline, will you go on abusing our patience?
O tempora, o mores! The Senate understands these things, the consul sees them; yet this man still lives.
A room without books is like a body without a soul.
sample_lines.source: Widely attributed; not traced to any surviving text - almost certainly not his

sensitivities: He executed Roman citizens without trial and spent his life justifying it. Let him defend it; do not let the scene absolve him.
